A 49-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease and end-stage renal disease requiring
hemodialysis through an internal jugular venous catheter is admitted to intensive care for acute
decompensated heart failure. The patient has a documented history of difficult venous access. On the
fourth hospital day, he develops fever (38.5°C/101.3°F) and chills. His vital signs show: pulse 92/min,
blood pressure 121/65mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The
catheter site shows erythema and tenderness on examination. Laboratory findings reveal elevated
leukocytes and C-reactive protein. Blood cultures from two peripheral sites demonstrate Gram-positive
cocci in clusters. What is the most appropriate next step in management? Answer Choices: (A)
Remove the central line and start IV caspofungin (B) Start empiric combination therapy with
vancomycin and cefepime (C) Remove the central line and start oral linezolid (D) Attempt central line
lock therapy with IV gentamicin (E) Remove the central line and start IV vancomycin (F) Place a new
central line at a different site and start IV vancomycin (G) Attempt central line lock therapy with IV
vancomycin (H) Await blood culture sensitivities before starting antibiotics (I) Start IV daptomycin and
maintain the central line (J) Start IV nafcillin and maintain the central line
 A. Remove the central line and start IV caspofungin
B. Start IV daptomycin and maintain the central line
C. Attempt central line lock therapy with IV gentamicin

D. Remove the central line and start IV vancomycin
E. Remove the central line and start oral linezolid
F. Start IV nafcillin and maintain the central line
G. Start empiric combination therapy with vancomycin and cefepime
H. Place a new central line at a different site and start IV vancomycin
I. Attempt central line lock therapy with IV vancomycin
J. Await blood culture sensitivities before starting antibiotics
